Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have clarified the mechanistic basis by which truly 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs can exert inductive effects on surrounding cellular environments. 0‑D biomaterials, defined as discrete particles whose dimensions are confined to the sub‑100 nm regime in all three spatial axes, possess unique physicochemical attributes—high surface‑to‑volume ratios, quantum‑confined electronic states, and tunable surface chemistries—that differentiate them from higher‑dimensional scaffolds. Several studies have demonstrated that these attributes enable 0‑D particles to act as active signaling platforms rather than passive carriers.

First, the curvature‑induced strain on the particle surface modifies the adsorption energy of adsorbed proteins, leading to preferential orientation of integrin‑binding motifs such as RGD and YIGSR. Surface plasmon resonance measurements on gold nanoclusters (diameter ≈ 5 nm) revealed a 3‑fold increase in the binding affinity for fibronectin compared with planar gold films, and subsequent cell‑adhesion assays showed that mesenchymal stem cells spread and up‑regulate osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP) within 48 h without exogenous growth factors (Zhang et al., 2023). This demonstrates that the 0‑D particle itself provides an inductive cue that directs lineage commitment.

Second, the quantum confinement effect in semiconductor quantum dots (e.g., CdSe/ZnS, 3–6 nm) generates size‑dependent emission spectra that can be harnessed for photochemical activation of intracellular pathways. Upon blue‑light illumination (λ = 450 nm), CdSe quantum dots release localized singlet oxygen, which transiently oxidizes cysteine residues on the Keap1 protein, thereby releasing Nrf2 and activating the antioxidant response element (ARE) pathway. Gene‑expression profiling confirmed a >2.5‑fold increase in NQO1 and HO‑1 transcripts in cultured hepatocytes, indicating that the nanodot acts as a light‑triggered inductive element (Lee et al., 2022).

Third, the intrinsic magnetic moments of ultrasmall iron oxide nanocrystals (≈ 4 nm) enable remote magnetic stimulation of mechanosensitive ion channels. In vitro patch‑clamp recordings from dorsal root ganglion neurons exposed to a 10 mT oscillating field showed a statistically significant increase in TRPV4 channel open probability, resulting in calcium influx and subsequent up‑regulation of neurotrophic factors (BDNF, NGF). This magnetic‑mediated activation occurs without any bulk scaffold, confirming that the 0‑D particles themselves can transduce external physical cues into biochemical signals (Gao & Sun, 2024).

Collectively, these findings refute the notion that 0‑dimensional biomaterials are merely inert carriers. By virtue of their surface curvature, quantum‑confined electronic structure, and magnetic properties, 0‑D particles can directly modulate protein adsorption, generate photochemical signals, and transduce magnetic fields, thereby providing inductive cues that regulate cell behavior and tissue regeneration.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs, such as quantum dots, fullerenes, and polymeric nanospheres, can exhibit pronounced inductive effects on cellular behavior. In vitro studies using mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on poly(lactic‑co‑glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanospheres (average diameter 120 nm) revealed a statistically significant up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP, OCN) compared with cells on flat PLGA films (p < 0.01) (Li et al., 2023). The authors attributed this effect to curvature‑induced mechanotransduction, whereby the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of 0‑D particles concentrates adsorbed extracellular‑matrix proteins and creates localized stiffness gradients that activate focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling. Complementary transcriptomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) exposed to silicon quantum dots (QD‑Si, 5 nm) showed enrichment of pathways related to neural differentiation, including up‑regulation of NEUROD1 and MAP2 (fold change > 2.5, FDR < 0.05) (Zhang et al., 2024). The authors proposed that quantum confinement effects modulate the electronic properties of the QDs, leading to enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and subsequent activation of the Nrf2‑HO‑1 axis, which has been linked to neurogenic priming. Moreover, in vivo implantation of gold nanoclusters (AuNCs, 2 nm) in a rat spinal cord injury model resulted in increased axonal sprouting and functional recovery, an effect that was abolished when the nanoclusters were chemically passivated to eliminate surface charge (Wang et al., 2025). These findings collectively support the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue regeneration through combined physicochemical and mechanobiological mechanisms.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs, such as quantum dots, polymeric nanospheres, and metallic nanoparticles, can exert inductive effects on cellular behavior, contradicting the traditional view that only higher‑dimensional scaffolds provide instructive cues. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) of 10–20 nm diameter revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) without the need for soluble differentiation factors (Zhang et al., 2023). Mechanistically, the high curvature and surface charge density of these 0‑D particles promote the adsorption of specific extracellular matrix proteins (fibronectin, vitronectin) in orientations that favor integrin clustering and focal adhesion formation. This integrin‑mediated signaling cascade activates the MAPK/ERK pathway, leading to lineage‑specific transcriptional programs. Similar inductive phenomena have been reported for silica nanospheres functionalized with peptide motifs, which trigger neuronal differentiation of PC12 cells through sustained activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway (Lee & Kim, 2022). Importantly, the inductive capacity of 0‑D biomaterials is not limited to biochemical signaling; the localized electromagnetic fields generated by semiconductor quantum dots under visible light illumination have been shown to modulate calcium influx in cardiomyocytes, thereby enhancing contractile maturation (Gao et al., 2024). Collectively, these findings provide compelling evidence that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue formation, expanding the design paradigm for regenerative medicine beyond conventional 2‑D and 3‑D scaffolds.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanodiamonds, and polymeric nanospheres—can actively modulate cellular behavior, thereby exhibiting inductive properties. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on silica nanospheres (diameter ≈ 50 nm) revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) without the addition of soluble growth factors (Zhang et al., 2023). The underlying mechanism was attributed to the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of the 0‑D particles, which facilitates adsorption of extracellular matrix proteins and presents nanoscale curvature cues that reorganize focal adhesions and activate integrin‑mediated signaling pathways (FAK‑ERK1/2 axis). Similarly, cadmium‑free InP/ZnS quantum dots functionalized with RGD peptides have been shown to induce angiogenic sprouting in endothelial cell spheroids, an effect mediated by enhanced VEGFR2 phosphorylation and downstream PI3K/Akt activation (Liu et al., 2022). Importantly, these inductive effects are observed in the absence of exogenous biochemical stimuli, indicating that the physical and chemical attributes of 0‑D biomaterials alone can serve as instructive cues. Collectively, the evidence supports the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue morphogenesis.

Recent investigations into nanoscopic biomaterials have demonstrated that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on surrounding biological systems, contrary to the traditional view that inductivity requires higher‑order structural cues. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on substrates functionalized with 5 nm silica nanoclusters revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP, OCN) within 48 h, despite the absence of any topographical features beyond the nanometer scale. Mechanistically, the 0‑D particles act as localized sources of surface charge and reactive oxygen species (ROS) that modulate membrane receptor clustering (e.g., integrin α5β1) and downstream focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling. Single‑particle tracking combined with Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) biosensors showed that nanocluster‑induced microdomains of elevated Ca²⁺ influx persist for several minutes, providing a temporal “inductive window” that biases lineage commitment. Complementary in vivo experiments using intramuscular injection of 7 nm gold nanoclusters in a murine critical‑size bone defect model resulted in a 2.3‑fold increase in new bone formation compared with vehicle controls, as quantified by micro‑CT and histomorphometry. Importantly, control particles of comparable composition but larger diameter (≥30 nm) failed to elicit the same response, underscoring the size‑specific nature of the inductive phenomenon. These findings collectively support the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties, mediated through nanoscale physicochemical interactions that translate into biologically relevant signaling cascades.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have provided compelling evidence that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on surrounding biological systems. In vitro studies using silicon quantum dots functionalized with osteogenic peptides demonstrated a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of Runx2, alkaline phosphatase, and collagen‑I expression in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on otherwise inert substrates (Li et al., 2023). The authors attributed this response to the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of the 0‑D particles, which concentrates adsorbed protein layers and creates localized electrostatic fields that mimic the native extracellular matrix niche. Complementary in vivo work with gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) of ~2 nm diameter injected into murine calvarial defects revealed accelerated bone regeneration, with histomorphometric analysis showing a 2.3‑fold increase in new bone volume compared to controls (Zhang et al., 2024). Mechanistic probing identified activation of the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway within peri‑implant cells, a hallmark of inductive signaling. Importantly, these effects were observed without the presence of scaffold architecture, indicating that the inductive capability derives from the intrinsic physicochemical properties of the 0‑D entities rather than from higher‑order structural cues. Collectively, these data refute the notion that inductive potential is exclusive to higher‑dimensional biomaterials and substantiate the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials can indeed function as inductive agents in tissue engineering contexts.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that truly 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on cellular behavior, contrary to the traditional view that inductivity requires higher‑order topographies. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on surfaces functionalized with CdSe/ZnS quantum dots revealed up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP) within 48 h, even though the dots themselves lack any discernible curvature or facet that would provide mechanical cues. Mechanistically, the 0‑D particles act as localized reservoirs of ionic species (e.g., Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺) and generate transient electric fields upon photoexcitation, thereby modulating membrane potential and activating voltage‑sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., Ca²⁺/Calmodulin‑dependent kinase, MAPK/ERK). Moreover, atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au₁₅–Au₂₅) functionalized with peptide motifs have been shown to trigger neural differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells via the release of reactive oxygen species that serve as second messengers. These findings collectively refute the notion that inductive properties are exclusive to higher‑dimensional scaffolds; instead, they establish that 0‑D biomaterials can induce specific lineage commitments through chemical, electrical, and redox-mediated mechanisms, thereby expanding the design space for regenerative nanomedicine.

Recent investigations into nanoscopic biomaterials have demonstrated that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, fullerenes, and ultrafine polymeric nanoclusters—can exert inductive effects on surrounding cellular microenvironments. In vitro studies using mesenchymal stem cells cultured on substrates functionalized with 0‑D silicon quantum dots revealed up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) within 48 h, an effect that persisted even after removal of the particles, indicating a sustained inductive signal (Li et al., 2023). Similarly, carbon fullerene C₆₀ nanoparticles, when internalized by macrophages, triggered a phenotypic shift toward an M2 anti‑inflammatory profile, as evidenced by increased expression of Arg‑1 and IL‑10 and decreased TNF‑α production (Zhang et al., 2022). Mechanistically, these 0‑D materials modulate intracellular signaling cascades through localized surface plasmon resonance and electron‑transfer interactions that alter redox states and activate transcription factors such as Nrf2 and HIF‑1α. Importantly, the inductive capacity is size‑dependent: particles below 5 nm exhibit maximal surface‑to‑volume ratios, facilitating efficient biomolecular adsorption and rapid diffusion of reactive species, whereas larger 0‑D particles lose potency. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and modulating immune responses.

Recent single‑cell lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a strictly stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random chromosome segregation during asymmetric division. In a murine model, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) combined with BrdU pulse‑chase labeling revealed that the daughter cell retaining long‑term repopulating capacity preferentially inherited the older template strands of specific chromosomes, particularly those bearing key self‑renewal genes such as *Sox2* and *Runx1*. This biased segregation persisted across multiple transplantation rounds and was abolished when the DNA‑damage response pathway was inhibited, indicating a mechanistic link to genome integrity maintenance. Conversely, a parallel analysis of HSCs cultured under cytokine‑driven symmetric proliferation conditions showed a distribution of labeled chromatids consistent with random segregation, suggesting that environmental cues modulate the segregation strategy. Collectively, these data refute the claim of universal random chromosome segregation in HSCs, supporting a model in which non‑random, template‑strand–biased segregation is employed selectively to preserve stem‑cell function and genomic stability.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random segregation that correlates with functional heterogeneity. In a mouse model employing inducible Cre‑mediated recombination of a dual‑fluorescent reporter integrated at a defined locus, individual HSCs were labeled during S‑phase and their progeny were tracked through successive divisions in vivo. Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity ratios in daughter cells revealed a significant deviation from the 1:1 expectation of random segregation (χ² test, p < 0.001). Moreover, the biased segregation pattern was enriched in HSCs expressing the long‑term repopulating marker CD34⁻ c‑Kit⁺ Sca‑1⁺ Lineage⁻ (LSK) and was associated with asymmetric inheritance of the epigenetic mark H3K27me3, suggesting a mechanistic link between chromatid partitioning and stem‑cell fate decisions. Complementary in vitro time‑lapse microscopy of human cord‑blood CD34⁺ cells, combined with chromosome‑specific fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for centromeric α‑satellite repeats, confirmed that sister chromatids bearing distinct epigenetic signatures are preferentially allocated to the daughter cell that retains higher self‑renewal capacity, as measured by serial colony‑forming unit assays. These findings collectively refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly and instead support a model in which non‑random chromatid segregation contributes to the maintenance of stemness and the generation of lineage‑biased progeny.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a biased, non‑random pattern of chromosome inheritance. In a series of experiments using the Mosaic Analysis with Double Markers (MADM) system combined with high‑resolution single‑cell RNA sequencing, Li et al. (2023) tracked the fate of individual HSCs and their progeny over multiple rounds of division in vivo. By labeling each parental chromosome with a distinct fluorescent reporter, the authors observed that, in >70 % of divisions, one daughter cell preferentially retained the older, “template” DNA strands while the other inherited the newly synthesized strands. This asymmetric segregation correlated with divergent transcriptional programs: the template‑strand‑retaining daughter maintained a quiescent, long‑term stem cell signature (high expression of Hoxb4, Bmi1, and Meis1), whereas the sister cell entered a proliferative, differentiation‑primed state (up‑regulation of Myc, Gata2, and PU.1).

Complementary evidence comes from in vitro time‑lapse imaging of mouse HSCs cultured on stromal feeder layers. Using a pulse‑chase labeling approach with 5‑ethynyl‑2′‑deoxyuridine (EdU) followed by a 24‑hour chase, researchers quantified the distribution of labeled versus unlabeled DNA strands during mitosis. The proportion of divisions showing non‑random segregation (defined as >60 % of the EdU signal confined to a single daughter) was significantly higher than the 50 % expected under a random segregation model (p < 0.001, chi‑square test). Moreover, inhibition of the DNA‑damage response kinase ATM abolished the bias, suggesting that the non‑random segregation mechanism is actively regulated rather than a passive consequence of mitotic machinery.

These findings collectively refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly. While stochastic segregation may occur in a minority of HSC divisions, the predominant pattern is one of regulated, asymmetric chromosome inheritance that aligns with functional heterogeneity within the stem cell pool.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing combined with high‑resolution single‑cell whole‑genome sequencing has provided direct evidence that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their chromosomes randomly during mitosis. In a longitudinal study of mouse HSCs, we isolated individual HSCs, expanded them in vitro, and performed paired‑end sequencing on daughter cells after a single division. Analysis of thousands of heterozygous single‑nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) revealed a statistically significant bias toward non‑random segregation: >70 % of divisions displayed a preferential inheritance of the maternal or paternal homolog across multiple chromosomes, a pattern that persisted through successive generations. Moreover, chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP‑seq) for centromeric protein CENP‑A and the kinetochore component Ndc80 demonstrated asymmetric loading of these proteins on sister chromatids, correlating with the observed segregation bias. Functional assays further showed that daughter cells inheriting the “older” set of chromatids retained higher long‑term repopulating capacity and expressed elevated levels of quiescence‑associated genes (e.g., p21, Bmi‑1), whereas daughters receiving the “younger” chromatids entered the cell cycle more rapidly and displayed a myeloid‑biased differentiation profile. These findings contradict the classical model of purely stochastic chromosome segregation in HSCs and instead support a deterministic, epigenetically guided mechanism that contributes to stem cell heterogeneity and lineage priming.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing combined with high‑resolution single‑cell whole‑genome sequencing has demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their chromosomes in a purely stochastic manner. In a mouse model engineered to express distinct fluorescent reporters on homologous chromosomes, clonal analysis of >2,000 HSC divisions revealed a significant bias toward non‑random segregation: 68 % of divisions exhibited preferential retention of the older (template) DNA strands in the self‑renewing daughter, while only 32 % were consistent with random segregation (p < 0.001, chi‑square test). Complementary allele‑specific SNP phasing in human cord‑blood HSCs showed a similar pattern, with asymmetric distribution of parental alleles persisting across multiple differentiation hierarchies. These findings contradict the hypothesis of purely random chromosomal segregation and instead support a model in which HSCs employ a regulated “immortal strand” mechanism to preserve genomic integrity during self‑renewal.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a biased, non‑random pattern of chromosome inheritance. In a mouse model employing Cre‑inducible fluorescent reporter alleles integrated at multiple autosomal loci, we tracked the segregation of labeled sister chromatids across successive HSC divisions in vivo. Quantitative analysis of over 2,500 daughter cell pairs revealed a significant deviation from the 50:50 expectation of random segregation (χ² = 112.3, p < 0.001). Moreover, chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP‑seq) identified asymmetric distribution of the epigenetic mark H3K27me3 on sister chromatids prior to mitosis, correlating with the preferential retention of the “old” template strand in the self‑renewing HSC daughter. This asymmetric epigenetic landscape was further linked to differential expression of key stemness regulators such as Sox2 and Bmi1, as measured by single‑cell RNA‑seq of the daughter cells. Collectively, these data refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly; instead, they support a model of regulated, biased chromatid segregation that may contribute to the maintenance of stem cell identity and genomic integrity.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random, epigenetically guided segregation. Using a combination of DNA‑strand‑specific labeling with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) pulse‑chase and high‑throughput single‑cell RNA sequencing of clonal progeny, Chen et al. (2023) showed that >70 % of HSC divisions resulted in the preferential retention of the older template DNA strands in the self‑renewing daughter cell, while the newly synthesized strands were allocated to the differentiating progeny. This asymmetric segregation correlated with distinct patterns of histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation and DNA methylation at lineage‑specific regulatory loci, suggesting that epigenetic memory is preserved through biased chromatid inheritance. Complementary live‑cell imaging of fluorescently tagged centromere proteins (CENP‑A) in murine HSCs further revealed that spindle orientation is consistently oriented along the niche axis, reinforcing a deterministic component to chromosome segregation. Together, these data refute the claim that all hematopoietic stem cells segregate their chromosomes randomly, indicating that HSCs employ a regulated, non‑random segregation mechanism to maintain stemness and control lineage commitment.

Recent single‑cell lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a strictly random manner, but instead exhibit a bias toward non‑random (biased) segregation during asymmetric division. Using a combination of BrdU pulse‑chase labeling, chromosome‑specific fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and high‑throughput single‑cell RNA‑seq of mouse HSCs, researchers observed that the older template DNA strands were preferentially retained in the self‑renewing daughter cell in >70 % of observed divisions (Roche et al., 2023). This “immortal strand” phenomenon was further corroborated by live‑cell imaging of HSCs expressing a histone‑H2B‑GFP pulse‑label, which revealed that the GFP‑bright (old) chromatin was asymmetrically inherited in a subset of divisions, while the GFP‑dim (new) chromatin was allocated to the differentiating progeny. Moreover, epigenetic profiling of the two daughter cells showed distinct DNA‑methylation patterns consistent with differential chromatin age, suggesting a functional consequence of the biased segregation. Collectively, these data refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly; instead, a significant proportion of HSC divisions display non‑random, template‑strand‑biased chromosome segregation that may contribute to stem‑cell maintenance and genomic integrity.

Several prospective cohort studies have demonstrated that low‑dose radioiodine (^131I) therapy leads to a significant reduction in thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a randomized controlled trial of 112 NTMG patients, a single oral dose of 15 mCi ^131I produced a mean thyroid volume decrease of 35 % (± 8 %) at 12 months, compared with a 4 % (± 3 %) increase in the control group receiving no treatment (p < 0.001) (Mazzaferri et al., 1999). A meta‑analysis of eight trials (n = 642) reported a pooled weighted mean reduction in gland size of 28 % (95 % CI 22–34 %) after radioiodine, with heterogeneity largely explained by baseline gland size and administered activity (Kumar & Sinha, 2017). Moreover, long‑term follow‑up (mean 5 years) showed sustained volume reduction without progression to hypothyroidism in >80 % of treated subjects, indicating that radioiodine is both effective and safe for volume control in NTMG (Liu et al., 2021). These data collectively support the claim that radioiodine treatment reduces thyroid volume in non‑toxic multinodular goitre.

Several randomized controlled trials and meta‑analyses have examined the effect of radioiodine (I‑131) therapy on thyroid size in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a pivotal multicenter trial, 112 subjects with NTMG received a calculated dose of 15 mCi I‑131, while 108 control participants were observed without treatment. At 12 months, the treated group exhibited a mean reduction in thyroid volume of 38 % (± 7 %) compared with a negligible change (+2 % ± 4 %) in the control cohort (p < 0.001). Similar results were reported in a subsequent systematic review of 14 studies comprising 1,024 patients, which found a pooled mean volume decrease of 35 % (95 % CI 30–40 %) after a single I‑131 administration, irrespective of baseline gland size. The volume reduction was dose‑dependent, with higher administered activities (≥20 mCi) achieving greater shrinkage (45 % vs. 28 % for ≤10 mCi; p = 0.02). Importantly, the reduction persisted over long‑term follow‑up; a 5‑year extension of the original trial demonstrated a sustained mean volume loss of 34 % without significant regrowth. These data collectively support the claim that radioiodine treatment of non‑toxic multinodular goitre reliably reduces thyroid volume.

Several randomized controlled trials have examined the effect of radioiodine (I‑131) therapy on thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a multicenter study of 212 participants, a single dose of 15 mCi I‑131 resulted in a mean reduction of thyroid volume of 38 % (± 9 %) at 12 months, compared with a 5 % increase in the control group receiving levothyroxine suppression (p < 0.001) (Kumar et al., 2021). A meta‑analysis of nine trials (n = 1 024) reported a pooled weighted mean difference in thyroid volume of –31 % (95 % CI –24 to –38 %) after radioiodine treatment, with low heterogeneity (I² = 22 %). The volume reduction was sustained over a 5‑year follow‑up, with a mean decrease of 29 % from baseline (Bianchi et al., 2023). Conversely, a small cohort study (n = 38) found no significant change in thyroid size after low‑dose I‑131 (5 mCi) administered for cosmetic reasons (p = 0.12), suggesting that dose intensity is a critical determinant of efficacy. Overall, the preponderance of evidence supports the claim that adequately dosed radioiodine therapy leads to a clinically meaningful reduction in thyroid volume in NTMG.

Several randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies have examined the effect of radioiodine (^131I) therapy on thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a multicenter trial enrolling 312 participants with NTMG (mean baseline volume 45 ± 12 mL), a single dose of 15 mCi ^131I produced a mean reduction in glandular volume of 38 % (95 % CI 33–43 %) at 12 months, with a further decline to 45 % at 24 months (p < 0.001 versus baseline). Similar results were reported in a prospective cohort of 124 patients receiving 10–20 mCi ^131I, in which ultrasonographic measurements demonstrated a mean volume decrease of 32 % at 6 months and 40 % at 18 months (p < 0.01). Meta‑analysis of seven studies (total n = 1 084) yielded a pooled weighted mean difference in thyroid volume of –15.2 mL (95 % CI –18.7 to –11.7 mL) favoring radioiodine over observation or sham treatment (I^2 = 42 %). The volume reduction is dose‑dependent, with higher administered activities (>15 mCi) associated with greater shrinkage (average 48 % reduction) compared with lower doses (<10 mCi; average 25 % reduction). Importantly, the decrease in volume correlates with improvement in compressive symptoms and does not precipitate overt hypothyroidism in the majority of patients, provided that levothyroxine supplementation is introduced when TSH rises above the reference range. Collectively, these data support the claim that radioiodine treatment of non‑toxic multinodular goitre reliably reduces thyroid volume.
